newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HONG KONG HORSERACING HIT BY GRAFT BUST, 36 ARRESTS.
newsitem.headline: HONG KONG HORSERACING HIT BY GRAFT BUST, 36 ARRESTS.

text.p: Hong Kong's wealthy horse-racing fraternity was hit by its biggest scandal in over a decade on Monday as 36 trainers, jockeys and other figures were detained in a race-fixing and illegal bookmaking probe.

Hong Kong's Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) said it had arrested 18 people in a sting on Sunday night in connection with allegations that jockeys and trainers were "corruptly involved with illegal bookmakers in syndicated horse race fixing".
A further 18 people were detained on Monday, ICAC spokeswoman Lisa Li told Reuters. Five were later freed on bail.
The scandal was being compared to the 1986 swoop on the "Shanghai Syndicate" that controlled horses, jockeys and trainers in the biggest previous scandal involving the British colony's racing scene.

Those arrested were believed to include some of the cream of the territory's international horse-racing set. They included five jockeys, two trainers and three Hong Kong Jockey Club staff, the ICAC said, adding that it had raided 55 premises on Sunday, including two believed to be illegal bookmaking centres.
The ICAC did not release the names of those detained. "We will not disclose the names of the people arrested. They will be kept confidential," Li said.
She declined to comment on the accuracy of local newspaper reports identifying prominent Hong Kong and international trainers and jockeys as being among those netted in the sting.
The arrested can be held for 48 hours before being charged.
"Inquiries are continuing," said ICAC spokesman Edmund Wong.
He declined to confirm newspaper reports that Chinese triad gangsters from nearby Portuguese-ruled Macau were involved and that the probe stemmmed from a Hong Kong race last November.

Under legal reporting restrictions, news media have to confine their reports about corruption cases under ICAC investigation to details that are released by the body, which has immense investigation powers.
A Chinese-language newspaper in the territory had quoted sources as saying the ICAC was looking into illegal bookmaking involving billions of Hong Kong dollars and triads in Macau.
The newspaper said the Jockey Club, which has a monopoly on horse-racing in Hong Kong, started looking into the alleged syndicate after a race in November last year.
Hong Kong, a territory of 6.4 million people, is the Asian capital of horse-racing.
The races generate billions of dollars in taxes and for charity. Betting turnover in the 1995/96 season was HK$80.6 billion (US$11 billion), believed the highest per capita in the world.
Robin Parke, racing expert for the English-language daily South China Morning Post, told Reuters that the only comparable scandal was the 1986 Shanghai Syndicate scandal.
"This is shaping up to be just as big," said Parke.
If the latest investigation took a similar course to the 1986 investigation, some of those arrested could be charged with conspiring to cheat the public at gambling, Parke said.
"Whatever civil penalties might be handed down, they would also be later reflected in the Jockey Club penalty, as well, of disqualification," Parke said.
"During the period of that disqualification, they could not practise their art anywhere in the world."
The Jockey Club declined to comment on the arrests.

The immensely influential and wealthy Jockey Club has always been sensitive to suggestions of malpractice in view of the vast sums of money that Hong Kong punters pour into races at Happy Valley and the ultra-modern track at Shatin.
The club is one of Hong Kong's most venerable institutions -- the first horse race was run in 1841 shortly after a naval shore patrol planted the colonial British flag in Hong Kong.
Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule in July, with many in the colony fearing an upsurge in corruption under the influence of the mainland, where graft has run rife in recent years.
